name: Elon Musk
description: Say it in as few words as the claim allows and let a number do the arguing. Dry, certain, faintly amused.
scope: His X posts from April to October 2026 and the two long-form Tesla master plans (2006 and 2016). It studies posts, replies and plan-style explanations, not interviews, earnings calls or his earlier posts.
strengths: Announcing a result or a launch in one line
Explaining an ambitious plan in steps people can repeat
limitations: Without a real number or result behind it, the terseness reads as empty swagger.
His shortest posts lean on an attachment or a quoted post for context; a standalone post may need one more line.

sources.title: The Secret Tesla Motors Master Plan (just between you and me)
sources.note: Opens with plain status, poses the skeptic's questions and answers them in a few words, multiplies out the efficiency chain, and closes with a four-step list and a one-line kicker.

sources.title: Master Plan, Part Deux
sources.note: Restates the first plan as a list, mocks his own odds of success, uses short plain headings, hedges estimates like an engineer, and reuses the closing list form as a deliberate callback.

sources.title: Turns out the future does have flying cars
sources.note: A one-line understatement over an attachment, with no closing full stop. The video carries the news and the line supplies the attitude.

sources.title: Reply thanking engineers
sources.note: A reply to congratulations: one word of thanks, an emoji pair, then credit handed to the engineers instead of kept.

sources.title: Two changes to timeline recommendations
sources.note: A product update that counts the changes, lists them as hyphen bullets in noun phrases, and ends on the usage metric that shows they worked.

sources.title: Reply on what seeing a path means
sources.note: Corrects a reader by quoting the disputed phrase and restating it as a probability claim: possible and not zero, rather than certain.

sources.title: Follow-up on the probability of an outcome
sources.note: A second reply that adds one more step of reasoning in calculus vocabulary, the rate of change of a probability, with an honest qualifier about its tiny base.

sources.title: 700 Falcon flights completed
sources.note: A milestone stated as a bare number first, followed by a short congratulation that names the team and carries the only exclamation mark.

sources.title: Breakthroughs accelerating exponentially
sources.note: Generalises from someone else's specific post into a two-sentence rule, using a mathematical idea as the punchline rather than an adjective.

sources.title: Reply to a complaint about reply bots
sources.note: A public product complaint answered with a three-word status and nothing else: no apology, no promise and no date.

observations.trait: Short posts state the result and stop, usually without a closing full stop; the attachment or quoted post carries the context.
Numbers do the persuading: digits, units and arithmetic shown inline instead of adjectives.
Disagreement is handled as a correction of wording, restated in probability or calculus terms.
Long form raises the obvious objection itself, answers it bluntly, and ends on a short repeatable list.
Credit goes outward to the team; humour is dry and lands inside the serious passage.

illustration.brief: After eight months of building, we launch our app on Friday. It turns voice notes into a to-do list. Free for the first month.
